study: HS-2 Hakes-Sauer verdict: run-value benchmark attempt + formal proportionality test

benchmark_attempt.dedupe_note: 29 duplicated 2026 team rows in the committed table differ only in the payroll cell (one copy stores a raw tuple string); batting fields are identical across copies. Deduped to 480 unique team-seasons (30 teams x 16 seasons), keeping the numeric-payroll copy.
benchmark_attempt.dependent_variable: team runs scored per PA (R / PA)
benchmark_attempt.ecological_limit: Team-season aggregates: OBP and SLG co-move through batting average (r = 0.77), so the aggregate regression splits their joint variation and prices a point of OBP lower than event-level linear-weights analyses of individual plate appearances do. This is the ratio the repo's committed data supports — an aggregate benchmark, not an event-level run value. The 60-game 2020 season is included; all variables are per-PA rates and season fixed effects absorb each season's run environment.

S.salary_basis: Spotrac-basis file data/salaries_2026.json, salary_2026 field (2027 payroll basis per Cycle 41)

quartile_contrast_from_hs1.note: Descriptive quartile contrast — NOT a price effect; no controls for age, position, or contract timing.

verdict.body: The formal Hakes–Sauer proportionality test, run against a run-value benchmark derived from 480 committed team-seasons (2011–2026; benchmark OBP/SLG run-value ratio 0.94, 95% CI 0.72–1.17), cannot reject correct proportional pricing of OBP relative to SLG in either salary sample (Sample S, Spotrac basis, n = 60: p = 0.42; Sample C, Cot's LRP-2027, n = 82: p = 0.90). It also cannot reject large mispricing in either direction — at these samples every economically plausible pricing ratio survives the test, so the samples lack the power to settle the question. The descriptive contrast is consistent across both salary bases: top-quartile contact hitters cost about half the median dollars per WAR of the bottom quartile (0.54x in S, 0.53x in C) — a contrast, not a price effect. The defensible claim is that these skills are persistent and cap-efficient with low variance — not that they are proven undervalued. Design limit: an active-contract cross-section, not Hakes & Sauer's newly-signed free agents; skills are 2027 projections.
verdict.short: INCONCLUSIVE on mispricing. The formal proportionality test (run-value benchmark from 480 team-seasons, ratio 0.94) cannot reject correct OBP-vs-SLG pricing in either salary sample (S, n = 60, p = 0.42; C, n = 82, p = 0.90) — and cannot reject large mispricing either: the samples lack power. What stands: the skills persist, and top-quartile contact hitters cost about half the median $/WAR of the bottom quartile on both salary bases — a descriptive contrast, not a price effect. The claim is persistent + cap-efficient + low-variance, not proven undervaluation. Design limit: active contracts, not newly-signed free agents.
verdict.design_limit: active-contract cross-section, not newly-signed FAs; skills are Marcel 2027 projections; Sample S at the n=60 power floor (24 of 30 teams)
